comparison: Both evaluate Sam68's spatiotemporal expression pattern (C1, C25-C32, C118). OpenEval finds the evidence strongly supportive based on qPCR, Western blot, and immunofluorescence data. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, requesting additional immunofluorescence staining at E13.5 and quantification improvements, indicating they want stronger evidence for these expression pattern claims.

Both evaluate the in vivo NPC proliferation and differentiation phenotype (C2-C3, C34-C42, C119-C120). OpenEval finds extensive support from BrdU labeling, Ki67 staining, and cell-type markers. Peer reviewers explicitly state the authors 'convincingly show' the early cell cycle exit and neural differentiation, indicating strong agreement on these core findings.

OpenEval R2 includes cortical expansion claims (C43-C45) as part of the broader in vivo phenotype and finds them supported. Peer R3 specifically addresses cortical expansion (C43-C46) with uncertainty, raising critical concerns about whether size and sex of mice were properly controlled, given that Sam68-/- mice are smaller.

Both evaluate in vitro neurosphere and differentiation phenotypes (C47-C55, C121). OpenEval finds strong support from neurosphere assays, clonogenic assays, and differentiation experiments. Peer reviewers acknowledge these findings in their summary without raising concerns, indicating agreement on the in vitro characterization.

Both evaluate the splicing-sensitive exon array data and Sam68's role in expression/splicing regulation (C56-C62, C122). OpenEval finds the microarray analysis supportive of Sam68's dual role. Peer reviewers acknowledge the approach and focus on ALDH1A3 without raising methodological concerns, indicating acceptance of these findings.

Both evaluate the Aldh1a3 3'-end processing mechanism (C4-C5, C63-C68, C108). OpenEval finds strong mechanistic evidence from microarray, 3'-RACE, DRB assays, and CLIP. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, requesting Northern blot analysis because RT-PCR cannot prove absence, and questioning why Sam68 wasn't observed binding the dPAS in exon 13.

Both evaluate the truncated ALDH1A3 protein and its properties (C69-C76, C124-C125). OpenEval finds support from Western blot, ALDEFLUOR assays, and activity assays showing the truncated form is inactive. Peer reviewers express uncertainty about an apparent contradiction between decreased protein and increased transcript, requesting experiments with autophagy/proteasome inhibitors to clarify the truncated isoform's fate.

Both evaluate the correlation between Sam68 and Aldh1a3 expression patterns (C80-C84, C109-C110). OpenEval finds support from RT-PCR during differentiation and correlation analysis across brain regions. Peer reviewers request quantification of Sox2+/ALDH1A3+ cells (also addressing C79, C123), indicating uncertainty about the spatial restriction and correlation claims.

Both evaluate the ALDH1A3 rescue experiments (C6, C85-C87, C111). OpenEval finds strong evidence from gain- and loss-of-function experiments. Peer reviewers find the rescue 'convincing' but express uncertainty by requesting additional negative control experiments with the truncated isoform to fully support specificity.

Both evaluate the link between ALDH1A3, glycolytic metabolism, and NPC self-renewal (C7, C88-C94, C112-C113, C126). OpenEval finds strong support from lactate assays, ALDH inhibition, and rescue experiments. Peer reviewers explicitly state the authors 'convincingly show' this connection and 'demonstrate' the requirement for high ALDH1A3 activity in maintaining the stem cell pool, indicating strong agreement.

Both evaluate the integrative model (C8, C114-C116). OpenEval finds the Sam68→ALDH1A3→glycolysis→NPC self-renewal pathway well-supported by convergent evidence. Peer reviewers summarize the model positively, stating the authors 'convincingly show' the mechanism, indicating acceptance of the overall proposed pathway. OpenEval R10 also includes C8 which appears in Peer R10 with minimal overlap.

OpenEval R11 evaluates background/context claims from published literature (C9-C24, C95-C107). No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers typically do not evaluate background claims that are supported by citations rather than novel experimental findings.
OpenEval R12 evaluates TUBB3 expression as a differentiation control (C33). No corresponding peer review evaluation found; this control marker was not specifically discussed by reviewers.

OpenEval R13 evaluates TBR1 as a post-mitotic neuron marker (C39). This claim appears in Peer R2's broader evaluation of the in vivo phenotype (C2-C3, C34-C42, C119-C120) where it is accepted without specific comment as part of the convincing demonstration of neural differentiation.

OpenEval R14 evaluates body weight control (C46) as supporting specificity of cortical phenotype. Peer R3 addresses cortical expansion including C46, but raises concerns about whether size and sex were properly controlled, directly questioning the adequacy of this control.

OpenEval R15 evaluates ALDH1A3/SOX2 co-localization (C79, C123). Peer R8 addresses these claims as part of their request for quantification of Sox2+/ALDH1A3+ cells, expressing uncertainty about the spatial restriction and co-localization evidence.

OpenEval R16 evaluates the speculative connection to neurological disorders (C117) as uncertain, noting it extends beyond experimental data. Peer R11 includes C117 in their overall positive summary of the model without specifically addressing the speculative nature of the disease connection.

OpenEval R17 evaluates the hypothesis motivating microarray experiments (C122). Peer R5 includes C122 as part of their acceptance of the microarray approach and identification of dysregulated genes, indicating the hypothesis was appropriately tested.

OpenEval R18 evaluates the claim about Sam68 affecting a small number of genes compared to U1 snRNP (C127). No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers did not specifically comment on this comparative inference.
